passages.original: alio deinde ac posteriori loco hanc, quae de Vitali agit, epistolam recitat sub hac inscriptione : Incipit rescriptum Damasi papae ad petitum Hieronymi ad Paulinum epi- scopum, atque alit hisce similes codices proferri possent· Alterum vero quod ex iisdem adverti, illud est, quod codex uterque auctior est, quam impressi libri, integra scilicet periodo illa, qua Dominicus homo, cujus Rufinus meminit, expressus est, ac deest in editis. Hos igitur ego codices, Isidorum praeterea Mercatorem, Baro- nium, ac Sarazanium secutus sum, ac epistolam hanc ab ea, quae Damasi confessio, seu regula fidei dicitur, se- paratam edidi : sed ad hoc me impulerunt praeterea ra- tiones aliae, quas cum attulerim cap.
passages.english: Then, in another and later place, it gives this letter, which deals with Vitalis, under this heading: "Here begins the rescript of Pope Damasus, at the request of Jerome, to Bishop Paulinus"; and other manuscripts similar to these could be cited. The second thing that I noticed from the same [manuscripts] is this: that each manuscript is fuller than the printed books, namely by that whole sentence in which the "Lordly man" (Dominicus homo), whom Rufinus mentions, is expressed, and which is missing in the editions. I have therefore followed these manuscripts, and besides them Isidore Mercator, Baronius and Sarazanius, and have published this letter separately from the one which is called the Confession of Damasus, or Rule of Faith; but other reasons also moved me to this, which, since I have set them out in chap.
passages.notes: "alit" read as "alii" (scanning error). "Dominicus homo" is a christological term ("the Lord's man" / "lordly man") referring to Christ's humanity; kept in Latin. The sentence breaks off mid-reference; the context after shows it continues "10 and 15".
